doc.title: Urbie Green interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995

title: The Basie rhythm section and playing softer
summary: Praises the Basie rhythm section's time at the A&R studio and says playing less loudly makes a band sound bigger than blasting like Woody's.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you about your work with the Basie band. Can you tell us about the sound or the feel of that rhythm section? Because everybody says they like that rhythm section, that was the rhythm section, the big band rhythm section.

Yeah, well anytime I ever do high school and college clinics, I always tell them to listen to the Basie band, well the whole band, but particularly the rhythm section. It’s just an example of the way it’s supposed to go, I mean in that type of music anyway. And I remember during the period that we played with them, we were normally recording at the A&R Studio on 48th Street, which was a very small room, probably about half as big as this room, and the whole band in there, and the time was so precise you know. And I just left, I mean before I went to New York to do studio work I had played with Woody Herman and Gene Krupa’s bands for, well Gene for about four years and Woody for three years, and although those bands always admired the Basie and Ellington bands very much, it was just a little different. Sometimes I always noticed that the Basie band didn’t really play as loud as you think they’re playing either, you know? Like we would get up with Woody and we’d blast away all night and blow the walls out we thought. But sometimes if you play a little softer it sounds bigger, you know, than if you — the louder you play the thinner it gets. But if you just settle back a little bit it opens up a real wide horn sound.
Kind of it counts up like we ain’t really working or this ain’t hard?
Yeah. It sounds bigger than when you’re blasting away.

Yeah. And a lot of it has to do with the balance too of being able to hear everything. You know I’m sure when a band is wailing away it’s tough. The piano disappears and certain other parts of the music.
Well Basie could always find those holes anyway though.
Yeah. He’d choose his moments wouldn’t he?
Well I think the Basie band did leave a lot of open spots.
